newsitem.title: USA: Government charges Reynolds on "Joe Camel" ads.
newsitem.headline: Government charges Reynolds on "Joe Camel" ads.

text.p: The government charged Wednesday that R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co.'s "Joe Camel" cartoon ads illegally promote its "addictive and dangerous" cigarettes to children and adolescents.

The Federal Trade Commission voted 3-2 to bring the cigarette maker before an administrative law judge, demanding the company cease targeting children under 18. The FTC would also require the tobacco maker to run a public education campaign that discourages young people from smoking.

At the White House, spokesman Barry Toiv welcomed the move, saying, "The president has been working very hard to protect kids from the dangers of smoking. We're very happy to see any action that will help in that effort."
But R.J. Reynolds labeled the charges "unprecedented, unfounded and unwarranted," declaring: "We will vigorously defend this complaint and we fully expect to prevail."

Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., said the demand it conduct an education campaign to discourage children from smoking exceeds "any reasonable interpretation of the FTC's authority" and would force the company to incur a burden not shared by its competitors.

The Federal Trade Commission -- an independent agency whose members are appointed by the president for seven-year terms -- reversed a 3-2 decision from 1994 not to act against the "Joe Camel" campaign.

FTC Consumer Protection Director Jodie Bernstein said "new evidence" had promoted the change. But it also occurred after a change in the make-up of the commisson, which has become more aggressive since two members appointed by Clinton joined.

"R.J. Reynolds has conducted one of the most effective advertising campaigns in decades," said Bernstein. "Joe Camel has become as recognisable to kids as Mickey Mouse. Yet the campaign promotes a product that causes serious injury, addiction and death."
"Joe Camel" appears in ads and on watches, T-shirts, lighters and other premiums, but Bernstein said the FTC wants to limit it to bars and other places permitting adults only.
The latest decision by the FTC comes as separate and unrelated negotiations on tobacco resulted in an apparent agreement on smoking advertisements.

"If we have our way, and I think we will, you won't be seeing any cigarette advertising," Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore told reporters in Chicago, where he addressed a conference with public health groups to discuss progress at the months-long negotiations with cigarette manufacturers.
Asked about the negotiations, Bernstein said the FTC was a law enforcement agency and could not act based on the uncertain outcome of the talks.

One of the two dissenting commissioners, Rodney Starek, said he was concerned about the harm that smoking poses to children. "But I also take seriously the statutory limits on the commission's authority."
Some on Capitol Hill have a broader view of government authority and had pressured the Federal Trade Commission to renew its Joe Camel investigation.
Last summer 67 House members led by Indiana Democrat Tim Roemer demanded the FTC re-open its "Joe Camel" investigation. That petition was augmented by a letter last month from nine senators.

"The peddling of illegal drugs to children cannot be tolerated," the Senate letter said, noting that Camel's share of the youth market has jumped from less than 3 percent to as high as 16 percent since the "Joe Camel" campaign started.
Bernstein would not say specifically if other tobacco commpanies are being investigated for marketing to children.
